pages.spec: Know what programming is, who the first programmer was, and why programming skills are useful
pages.summary: Programming (coding) is writing instructions in a language computers understand. Ada Lovelace was the first programmer; there are about 700 languages, and programming builds skills used in many jobs.

blocks.text: What is programming?

[[Programming]] is everything involved in making, controlling and communicating with digital devices. It is often called **coding**, because it involves writing in a language that computers can understand. This lets us develop devices, apps and technology in our own way. A [[programmer]] is a person who writes code for a device and also **tests** the code to make sure it is fully functional (works properly).
The first computer programmer

**[[Ada Lovelace]]** (1815–1852) is famous as the first computer programmer. She worked with **Charles Babbage**, who designed the first general-purpose computer, the **Analytical Engine**. In 1843 Ada wrote what is seen as the first algorithm intended to be carried out by a machine, to calculate a series called the Bernoulli numbers. She also saw that machines could go beyond pure calculation, for example to create music. That is why she is cited as the first computer programmer.

**How many programming languages?** There are roughly **700** programming languages in use today. They exist because different jobs need different features. Some are very good for app development, web development, phone and tablet development, operating system development or general software development. Famous ones include Python, Java, JavaScript and C#.
Jobs in programming

IT jobs have grown considerably every year and are often very well paid. Programming leads directly to jobs such as: It also helps in careers that are not directly in IT: **medicine and dentistry** (analysis skills), the **army** (problem solving), **analyst** roles (analysing everything) and **marketing** (all of the above). Jobs that use programming directly include:

items: Software engineer
Network architect
IT project manager
Database administrator
Web developer
Systems analyst
Mobile app developer
IT consultant
Technical sales rep
Support analyst
Cyber security specialist
Social media manager

blocks.text: **Why learn programming?** Programming lets you give machines instructions, but it also teaches four key thinking skills you will use for the rest of your life:

head: Skill
What it means
rows: Pulling information out of a scenario to understand the problem, so you can create sensible solutions.
Working with ideas (concepts) rather than physical things.
Seeing relationships, and the consequences of actions that haven't happened yet.
Finding solutions to anything, and thinking outside the box (forward thinking).

blocks.text: Programming you already know

In ICT you have used **Scratch** and **BBC micro:bits** (drag-and-drop, event-based programming) and **HTML** web design, where you met a lot of computational thinking. You have also used the three basic programming concepts in other subjects:

head: Concept
Meaning
Where you met it
rows: [[Instructions|Sequence]] in a logical order, one after the other. An algorithm is a sequence of instructions.
The program decides whether a line or group of lines should be run, usually with an IF statement.
Repeating steps using loops: count-controlled, condition-controlled or infinite.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Programming (coding) means writing instructions in a language a computer understands.
A programmer writes and tests code.
Ada Lovelace, who worked with Charles Babbage on the Analytical Engine, was the first programmer.
There are about 700 programming languages, each suited to different jobs.
Programming builds analysis, abstract thinking, pattern recognition and problem-solving skills.
The three basic concepts are sequence, selection and iteration.

pages.spec: Know what C# is, what a compiler does and how Visual Studio (an IDE) helps you write code
pages.summary: C# is a high-level, strongly typed language made by Microsoft. A compiler turns it into binary, and we write it in an IDE such as Visual Studio, starting a Console App project.

blocks.text: C#: a high-level language

At ERGS we learn **[[C#]]** (pronounced 'C sharp'). It was written by Microsoft, is versatile, relatively easy to learn and has lots of documentation. It is used by companies like Microsoft and NASA, and is the main language of the **Unity** game engine, used to build games such as **Pokémon Go** and **Among Us**. The Stack Overflow website was built with ASP.NET, which also uses C#. C# is an object-oriented language that runs on Microsoft's **.NET** framework. You can use it to make Windows applications, websites and web services, mobile apps, video games, AR and VR, and much more.

Computers only understand binary. A [[compiler]] is the program that converts our human-readable code into the binary code the computer understands. This process is called **compiling**. We don't usually write in binary!
A strongly typed language
C# is **[[strongly typed]]**: you must say what type of data each variable holds before you use it. It means writing a bit more code, but has long-term benefits:

items: **Built-in documentation**: you can see how each data type works.
**Increased readability**, helping programmers work in teams.
**IntelliSense**: predictive text for code.
**Help with debugging**: it knows what can and can't happen with a data type before you even run your code.

blocks.text: Visual Studio: an IDE

Programmers don't write code in any old application. Basic packages like Notepad exist, but most use an [[IDE]] (Integrated Development Environment), which brings all the tools for viewing, writing, testing and running code together in one place. We use **Visual Studio**. Its features include:

items: **Line numbering**: tells lines apart in long programs and shows where errors are.
**Colour coding of keywords**, and coloured underlines: a **red underline** shows a syntax error.
**Collapsible code sections**: make large programs easier to view.
**Clipboard**: copy and paste.
Access to objects, methods and properties while you design.

blocks.text: To start: choose **Create a new project**, pick the **Console App** template (make sure it is the **C#** version), enter a project name with no spaces and click **Create**. A [[console]] application uses a text-only window, so we can focus on the fundamentals of C#.

School computers are managed by C2K, which limits what can be coded on them to keep them secure. In Year 10 you can practise in an online tool such as dotnetfiddle.net and Codecademy's *Learn C#* course; at GCSE you use a virtual machine.

blocks.title: Key points
items: C# is a high-level, strongly typed language made by Microsoft; Unity games such as Pokémon Go use it.
High-level languages are close to English; low-level languages are close to binary.
A compiler converts human-readable code into binary.
Strong typing gives documentation, readability, IntelliSense and help with debugging.
An IDE such as Visual Studio has line numbers, colour coding, red error underlines and collapsible code.

practice.a: Any two: built-in documentation (1); increased readability for teams (1); IntelliSense/predictive text (1); help with debugging before the code runs (1).

pages.spec: Write, run and comment a first C# console program using Console.WriteLine()
pages.summary: Every C# console program has the same structure, starting in the Main method. Console.WriteLine() shows text, every statement ends with a semicolon, and // starts a comment.

blocks.text: The program structure

blocks.title: Program.cs
blocks.output: Hello World!

blocks.text: Think of it like an author writing a series of books:

items: `using System;` says 'we're going to use some premade tools'.
`namespace myFirstProgram` is the name of the **book series**. Its `{` and `}` show where the series starts and ends.
`class Program` is **one book** in the series, with its own `{` and `}`, inside the series.
`static void Main(string[] args)` is a **chapter**. Every program starts in this Main method.
`Console.WriteLine("Hello World!");` is the **first sentence**.

blocks.text: In newer versions of Visual Studio, tick **'Do not use top-level statements'** when making the project, so you see this full structure.

**The magic command.** To make text appear on the screen we use `Console.WriteLine()`. `Console` is the **object**, `WriteLine` is the **method**, the text in speech marks is the **message**, and the `;` is the **line terminator**. Every instruction (statement) must end with a [[semicolon]], like a full stop at the end of a sentence.

To run your program, click the green **Start** (play) button. If there are errors in the **Error List** at the bottom, the program won't run: treat them as clues to a puzzle. For example, 'error CS1002: ; expected' means you are missing a semicolon at the end of the line.

My favourite sport is Gaelic football

blocks.text: Comments

A [[comment]] is text in a program that the computer ignores. Comments explain what code does, help other people understand it faster, and let you switch off a line to see how the program runs without it. In C#, anything after `//` on a line, or between `/*` and `*/`, is a comment. Visual Studio shows comments in **green**.

blocks.output: Comments are ignored

head: Key term
Meaning
rows: The text-based window where our program output appears.
The set of rules defining how code must be written.
The character ( ; ) used to end a statement in C#.

blocks.title: Key points
items: using System; → namespace (series) → class (book) → Main method (chapter) → statements (sentences).
Console.WriteLine("text"); displays text in the console.
Every statement ends with a semicolon.
Errors in the Error List stop the program running; read them as clues.

pages.spec: Declare variables using the correct data type: int, double, string, char and bool
pages.summary: A variable is a named box in memory that holds data. In C# you must give it a data type and a name, e.g. int score = 50; The main types are int, double, string, char and bool.

blocks.text: The box analogy

A [[variable]] is like a storage box in the computer's memory (RAM). It holds data while the program is running, and it is called a *variable* because the value inside can change. To use a box you need two things:

items: A **name**: the label on the box (the variable name, also called an identifier).
A **[[data type]]**: what kind of thing fits inside the box, e.g. a whole number or text.

blocks.text: In C# you must state the data type **before** you can put anything in the box.

**Data types.** Data types tell the computer how data can be stored, what operations can be done with it, and which methods it can be used with. Without them, a computer might try something impossible, like squaring a piece of text, and that is how we get bugs. C# is also **statically typed**: it checks you used the correct types before the program even runs.

head: Type
What it holds
Example
Size
rows: Whole numbers (integers), about −2.1 billion to +2.1 billion
Numbers with a decimal point (about 15–16 significant digits, **not** just two decimal places)
Text: a sequence of characters, in double quotes
A single letter or symbol, in single quotes
blocks.caption: The most common data types

blocks.text: Other types you may meet: `long` (bigger whole numbers, 8 bytes), `float` (less precise decimals, 4 bytes), `decimal` (money values, 16 bytes) and `DateTime` (moments in time from 00:00:00 on 1 January 0001 to 23:59:59 on 31 December 9999). You don't need to learn the ranges, but always choose a type of suitable size.

**Declaring and assigning.** To create a variable, write the **data type**, then the **variable name**, then `=` and the **value**, then a semicolon: `int score = 50;`. Creating the variable is called **[[declaration]]**. The `=` is the **assignment operator**: the value on the right is stored in the variable on the left. Note that C# prints a `bool` as `True` or `False` with a capital letter.

blocks.title: Variables.cs
blocks.output:
41
Alice
19.99
A
True

blocks.text: Naming variables

items: Names can contain letters, numbers and the underscore `_`, and must start with a letter or underscore.
No spaces, full stops or symbols, and no **reserved keywords** (words C# already uses, like `int`, `class` or `lock`).
Use descriptive names: `firstName` and `lastName`, not `abc` or `xyz`.
Use **[[camelCase]]**: start lower case and give every new word a capital, e.g. `favouriteSport`, `isMember`.

blocks.text: Worksheet answers: Data Types and Variables

head: Question
Answer
rows: What two things must you define before you can put anything into a variable box?
`string`: stores text, such as a name.
`int`: stores whole numbers, such as a score.
`double`: stores decimal numbers, such as a weight of 52.7 kg.
Which command outputs text to the screen?
Which command waits for the user to type and press Enter?

A **variable** is a named location in the computer's memory used to store data. When you create a variable, you are allocating space in the computer's **memory**. Specifying the name and the data type for a new variable is known as **declaration**. To store a whole number like 25, you should use the **int** data type. If you need to store a decimal value like 19.99, the **double** data type is required. Any data captured from a user via `Console.ReadLine()` is treated as a **string**.

blocks.title: Key points
items: A variable is a named storage box in memory whose value can change.
Declare a variable with: data type, name, =, value, semicolon.
int = whole numbers; double = decimals; string = text in "double quotes"; char = one character in 'single quotes'; bool = true or false.
Use descriptive camelCase names with no spaces or symbols.
Reserved keywords cannot be used as variable names.

pages.summary: Join text and variables with + (concatenation). Data types matter because "10" + "10" gives "1010" but 10 + 10 gives 20. Most beginner errors are missing types, wrong types, bad names and missing semicolons.

blocks.text: **Displaying your data.** You can combine text and variables in `Console.WriteLine()` using the `+` symbol. Joining text together like this is called **[[concatenation]]**. If `string profession = "Coding Wizard";` then `Console.WriteLine("Hello " + profession);` outputs **Hello Coding Wizard**. Tip: Leave a space inside the speech marks (`"Hello "`), or the words will be squashed together: `HelloCoding Wizard`.
Coding challenge: Digital ID card

blocks.text: Put calculations in their own brackets: `(age + 10)`. Without them, `"I will be " + age + 10` joins the text "15" and "10" to give **I will be 1510**.
**Why bother with data types?** If we could make every variable a `string`, why does C# make us use `int` and `double`? Because computers process numbers differently from text:

blocks.title: WhyTypes.cs

items: With strings, `+` joins the text: "10" + "10" = "1010", not 20, so you can't do maths properly.
Using the right type saves memory and prevents errors in complex calculations.
The compiler can spot type mistakes before you run the program.

pages.spec: Get input from the user with Console.ReadLine() and convert it to the data type you need
pages.summary: Console.ReadLine() pauses the program until the user types and presses Enter, and always returns a string. Use Convert.ToInt32() or Convert.ToDouble() to turn input into numbers.

blocks.text: Imagine apps that didn't listen to you: no search bars, no login screens, no game controls. Boring! Useful software gathers data from the user and reacts to it. Interactive programs follow a simple flow: **Input → Process → Output**.
Capturing input with Console.ReadLine()
`Console.ReadLine()` pauses the program until the user types some text and presses **Enter**. You store what they typed in a variable: `string name = Console.ReadLine();`
`Console.ReadLine()` **always** returns a `string`, even if the user types a number. If you need to do maths with it, you must convert it.
**Converting data types.** Because C# is strongly typed, sometimes we need to change the type of a value. This is called **[[data type conversion]]**. There are two kinds:

head: Implicit conversion
Explicit conversion
rows: Happens automatically because no data is lost
You must ask for it, because data could be lost
int → double (a double can hold any int)
double → int using the cast operator `(int)`
`9.99` becomes `9` (the decimal part is chopped off, not rounded)

blocks.text: The most common way to convert input is with the `Convert.To…` methods. In `int myValue = Convert.ToInt32("42");` the value "42" is in double quotes, so the computer thinks it is text. `Convert.ToInt32` is a predefined method that turns the string into an integer. (The 32 means it is a 32-bit integer, which is what `int` is.) For decimals, use `Convert.ToDouble()`.

blocks.title: Converting.cs

blocks.text: Task: ask for a name and age, stored in myName and myAge

Check yourself (answers)

items: To store a person's name, you first declare a **string** variable, then use **Console.ReadLine()** to capture their typing.
If you wanted to store their age, you would declare a variable called `age` with a data type of **int**.
To output the value stored within a variable, you would use the **Console.WriteLine()** method.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Interactive programs follow Input → Process → Output.
Console.ReadLine() waits for the user to type and press Enter.
Console.ReadLine() always returns a string.
Convert.ToInt32() turns text into an int; Convert.ToDouble() turns it into a double.
Implicit conversion is automatic (int → double); explicit conversion uses a cast such as (int).

pages.spec: Use the arithmetic operators + - * / and %, and the shortcuts ++ and --
pages.summary: C# uses + - * / for maths and % for the remainder. Dividing two ints gives a whole number; use a double to get decimals. ++ adds 1 and -- takes 1 away.

blocks.text: Arithmetic operators
Programs often need to do calculations. [[Arithmetic operators|Arithmetic operator]] work on numbers (`int` and `double`) to create new values.

blocks.title: Arithmetic.cs

blocks.text: **Watch the data types.** When both numbers are `int`s, the answer is an `int`. 3 doesn't go into 5 evenly, but `5 / 3` still gives the whole number **1** (the remainder is thrown away). In `5 / 3.0`, one number is a `double`, so the answer takes the 'bigger' data type and is a `double`: **1.6666666666666667**.
`7 / 2` is **3**, not 3.5! If you want decimals, make at least one of the numbers a double: `7 / 2.0` = 3.5.
C# follows BIDMAS, just like Maths: `2 + 3 * 4` is 14, but `(2 + 3) * 4` is 20.

**Modulus %.** The [[modulus]] operator `%` gives the **remainder** after a division. It uses the percent sign but has nothing to do with percentages. It is useful for checking whether a number 'fits' into another: `17 % 2` is 1, so 17 is **odd**; `18 % 2` is 0, so 18 is **even**.

blocks.title: Worked example: sharing out
blocks.context: 62 pupils are going on a trip to the Marble Arch Caves, in minibuses that seat 15. How many full minibuses, and how many pupils are left over?
steps: So you need 4 full minibuses plus one more for the last 2 pupils.
blocks.answer: 62 / 15 = 4 full minibuses; 62 % 15 = 2 left over, so 5 minibuses are needed.

pages.spec: Use IF, ELSE IF and ELSE with comparison operators to make decisions
pages.summary: An IF statement runs a block of code only if a condition is true; ELSE runs if it is false. Conditions use comparison operators such as ==, !=, <, >, <= and >=.

blocks.text: Logic is about choices. An [[IF statement]] tells the computer to run a block of code **only if** a specific [[condition]] is true. This is [[selection]].

Unlike Maths, C# uses a **double equals** `==` to compare things. A single `=` only **assigns** a value. So `if (age = 18)` is **not** the correct way to check if someone is 18 (it won't even compile); use `if (age == 18)`.
**The code pattern.** The condition goes inside the round brackets. If it is true, the code inside the curly braces `{ }` runs. The optional **ELSE** part runs if the condition is false.

pages.spec: Use a FOR loop (count-controlled) and name its three parts
pages.summary: A FOR loop repeats code a known number of times. It has an initialiser (where the counter starts), a condition (how long to keep going) and an iterator (how the counter changes, e.g. i++).

blocks.text: **Why do we need loops?** Imagine printing 'Hello World' 1,000 times. You could copy and paste 1,000 lines, but what if you then needed to change the message? A [[loop]] lets you write a block of code **once** and run it as many times as needed. This is **[[iteration]]** (repetition).
Loops make code shorter, easier to read and easier to maintain. Remember **DRY**: **D**on't **R**epeat **Y**ourself.

blocks.text: The FOR loop

pages.spec: Use a WHILE loop (condition-controlled), choose between FOR and WHILE, and avoid infinite loops
pages.summary: A WHILE loop checks a condition and keeps repeating while it is true, so it suits situations where you don't know how many repeats are needed. If the condition never becomes false, you get an infinite loop.

blocks.text: **The WHILE loop.** A `while` loop is best for **indefinite** iteration, where we don't know how many times the code will run, like waiting for a user to enter the correct password. It checks the condition **before** running the code block. If the condition is true, the code runs, then it checks again. It keeps looping **until the condition is false**. It looks a lot like an IF statement, but instead of running once, it repeats. Here `!=` means **not equal to** (≠). In the password program below, we don't know how many times the user will get the password wrong, but the loop repeats until they enter the correct one.

blocks.title: Password.cs
blocks.output:

letmein
Incorrect Password! Try again
fermanagh
Incorrect Password! Try again
myPassword123
Access granted. Welcome!

blocks.text: Scratch has no WHILE block. Its **repeat until** block does the opposite: it keeps going *until* the condition becomes true, whereas a C# `while` keeps going *while* the condition is true.

blocks.text: Infinite loops

One of the biggest dangers of a WHILE loop is an [[infinite loop]]. **Explained to a 10-year-old:** it's like getting stuck on a roundabout and never being able to take the exit. It happens when the condition to stop the loop never becomes false, so the computer keeps running the same code forever. Eventually the program can freeze or crash.

A common cause is forgetting to update the variable inside the loop. In the password program, if you left out `myVar = Console.ReadLine();` inside the loop, a wrong password would print 'Try again' forever.
Infinite loops are sometimes useful, for example a traffic light system that must repeat forever:

pages.spec: Understand methods and objects, and plan, build and test a program using the core four skills
pages.summary: Methods are named groups of instructions that run when called, and can take parameters and return answers. Every program is built from the core four: variables, input/output, selection and iteration. Plan, build in small steps, keep code clean and test it.

blocks.text: **Methods.** A [[method]] is a small group of instructions that runs when it is **called** in the code. The code inside runs in sequence, and only when the method is called. `Main` is a method, and so are `Console.WriteLine()` and `Console.ReadLine()`.

items: You call a method using its name followed by brackets: `SayHello();`
If a method accepts an input, the value goes in the brackets. This input is called a **[[parameter]]**. When creating the method, you must state the data type it expects, e.g. `string name`.
A method can send an answer back to where it was called using `return`.

blocks.title: Methods.cs
blocks.output:
Let's say hello in C#
Hello you!
Hello Mr Butler
The answer is 11

blocks.text: C# programmers usually start method names with a capital letter (PascalCase), e.g. `SayHello`, and variable names with a small letter (camelCase), e.g. `firstName`.

**Objects and instances.** C# is an **object-oriented** language. Object-oriented programming is based on **[[objects|object (programming)]]**, which each have their own **properties** (attributes, i.e. data) and **methods** (things they can do), and which can interact with one another. Objects let us reuse code written for one object in another without rewriting it all.
You have met this idea in GameMaker: an object is a template and each instance is a copy placed in the game. In C#, a **class** is the template and each object made from it is an instance.

**The core four.** Whether you're designing the next viral game or a secure bank login, it all comes down to four building blocks. Programming is simply giving a computer a set of instructions to solve a problem.

Meaning
rows: A named container for data that can change.
Choosing which code to run based on a condition (IF).
A data type that can only be true or false.

blocks.text: Plan, build, tidy, test

items: **Plan first (flowchart).** Don't touch the keyboard yet! Sketch the flow: what variables do you need, where does the loop start, what condition triggers the IF? Code without a plan becomes 'spaghetti code' that is hard to fix.
**Build iteratively: code, test, repeat.** Declare variables first; get the input working; add the IF statements; wrap the code in a loop **last**, to avoid infinite loops while testing.

**Keep code clean.** Developers spend more time reading code than writing it. Indent code inside curly braces, use meaningful names (`number1`, not `xfgdfgd` or `var1`) and use `//` comments to explain tricky logic.

**Test and review.** Swap with a partner and try to break their program with unexpected input (e.g. letters when it asks for a number). Does the loop end correctly? Are the IF statements logical? Is the code easy to read?

items: A method is a named group of instructions that runs when called; parameters pass values in; return sends an answer back.
Objects have properties (data) and methods (actions); a class is the template.
The core four: variables, input/output, selection, iteration.
Plan with a flowchart before coding.
Build in small steps, keep code clean (indentation, names, comments) and test with unexpected inputs.

practice.a: Variables, e.g. int score = 10; (1). Input/output, e.g. Console.ReadLine()/Console.WriteLine() (1). Selection, e.g. an if/else statement (1). Iteration, e.g. a for or while loop (1).

practice.a: Indent code inside curly braces (1); use meaningful/descriptive variable names (1); add // comments to explain complex logic (1).

practice.a: A named group of instructions that only runs when it is called (1). Benefit: code can be reused without rewriting it / programs are easier to read (1).
